about.title: About
about.heading: About Logia
about.dek: A free, open library of Christian commentary, set verse by verse beside Scripture.
what: Logia sets each verse of the Bible beside what the church has said about it, from the early church to the 1800s. It is free to read, free to share, and its data is open for anyone to build on, in the spirit of Sefaria's library of Jewish texts.
about.name_note: These are the words of Romans 3:2 for “the oracles of God”, which the Open Word Bible renders “the very words of God”. Logia takes its name from them, and from Papias's lost *Exposition of the Logia of the Lord*, one of the first Christian commentaries.
about.voices: Logia takes no side where Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readings differ. Each commentator's words are kept whole, even where they are harsh or dated: a note may explain, but nothing is cut silently.
about.traditions: Traditions in the library so far
about.checked: Every excerpt is copied from a public-domain edition and never rewritten. These are the five steps each one goes through, shown for one real excerpt.
steps: A page scan on archive.org or a transcription on CCEL, published in 1930 or earlier.
The page Logia copies from is kept in the repository, with its address and when it was fetched.
A script finds each excerpt in its source: word for word, or in runs of six words for a scan.
Where a scan misread the printed page, the fix is a pair kept in the open data.
The excerpt appears on Logia beside the verse it comments on, linked to the full text.
about.trail_scan: Found in its source in runs of six words, as a page scan.
about.trail_digital: Found in its source word for word, as a transcription.
about.trail_fix: The scan read “{a}”; the page reads “{b}”.
about.steps_note: Every one of the {n} excerpts goes through these steps; {fixes} scan misreadings are corrected in all.
about.details_text: Every excerpt is copied from a public-domain edition, never rewritten, and the source text it came from is kept beside it. A script checks each excerpt against its source on every change: word for word for a transcription, and in runs of six words for a page scan, whose lines carry margin notes and running heads. Where a scan misread a letter (“Let ns” for “Let us”), the correction is listed openly and applied when the site is built.
bible: Logia reads the Open Word Bible, a CC0 translation from Hebrew and Greek with the reasoning behind every sentence. Logia never edits it: it is imported at a pinned version from the Open Word Bible's own repository.
languages: Logia starts in English. Each new language is translated from the best public-domain source, the original Greek, Latin or German where that is better than the English, and reviewed by native speakers before it is marked reviewed.
privacy: Reading Logia needs no account, and Logia sets no cookies of its own. If you sign in to save or like comments, you use your Open Word Bible account, and what you save is kept there.
about.privacy_counter: To learn which books and pages people read, Logia counts visits with GoatCounter. It sets no cookies, keeps no IP addresses and builds no profile of anyone; it records only the page, the site you came from, and your browser, screen size and country in general terms.
open: Copy, change and publish it, with no permission needed and no credit required.
Build on the site's code, keeping its licence notice.
The Open Word Bible, free in the same way.
about.open_note: The Greek and Hebrew word data and the cross-references carry their own licences, listed on the open data page.

about.cite_note: To quote one excerpt, use the Cite button beside it, which names the edition it was copied from.
about.help: A script checks every excerpt, but people catch what scripts miss.

about.thanks: Logia stands on the work of others.
thanks_sefaria: The example of an open library of commentary, for Jewish texts.
questions: Why only books published in 1930 or earlier?

So that every text is in the public domain in the United States and free for anyone to copy. Most later commentaries are still under copyright. Each work's page records its edition and what is still to be confirmed for other countries.
No. Spelling, punctuation and the translator's English are kept as printed. Only plain misreadings by a scanner are fixed, and every fix is listed.
Is any of it written by AI?

No commentary is. Every excerpt is copied from its edition and checked against it by a script. Where Logia adds writing of its own, such as a guide or a biography, it is marked as a draft until a person reviews it.
Why isn't my favourite commentator here?
Logia adds one commentary at a time, and only from an edition published in 1930 or earlier with a readable scan or transcription. You can suggest one above.
Yes. The commentaries are in the public domain and Logia's data is CC0, so you may copy them into a sermon, a class handout or an app without asking.
Why are there no modern commentators?
Logia holds only editions published in 1930 or earlier, so that every text is free to copy. Commentators who wrote later, and modern translations of older ones, are mostly still under copyright.
Is the Bible text a new translation?

Yes. Logia shows the Open Word Bible, a CC0 translation from the Hebrew and Greek. It is an AI draft that people are reviewing, as each verse page says. Logia never edits it: a problem with its wording is fixed in the Open Word Bible itself.
Does Logia take sides between the churches?

No. Where Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers differ, Logia shows every commentator it holds on the passage, in the order they lived, and keeps their words whole. Its own short notes say how the readings differ without choosing between them.

good-friday.name: Good Friday

easter.name: Easter Day
easter.intro: On Easter Day many churches read John's account of the empty tomb. The Revised Common Lectionary gives John 20:1–18, and the Roman Missal reads John 20:1–9 at the Mass of the day. This page shows John 20:1–18.

ai.title: How Logia uses AI
ai.heading: How Logia uses AI
ai.dek: No commentary on Logia is written by AI. AI helps to build the library and to draft Logia's own notes, and everything it drafts is marked until a named person reviews it.
ai.description: What on Logia is drafted with AI, how it is marked, and what AI is never used for.
ai.mark_draft_title: Drafted with AI and not yet reviewed by a person. Follow the link to read how Logia uses AI.
ai.mark_reviewed_title: Drafted with AI, then reviewed and approved by {name}. Follow the link to read how Logia uses AI.
marks: Drafted with AI and not yet reviewed. Read it as a first draft: check it against the sources it points to.
Drafted with AI, then read and approved by the person named. The mark keeps their name, so you know who checked it.
ai.marks_note: Text with no mark is copied from a printed edition: the commentators' own words, quoted whole.
never: It never writes commentary. Every excerpt is copied word for word from a public-domain edition, and a script checks it against the saved source on every change.
It never types Greek or Hebrew. Original-language words come from the printed edition or from the open Greek and Hebrew texts, as they read.
It never fixes a scan by guessing. A misread letter is fixed only where the printed page plainly says otherwise, and every fix is listed in the open data.
It never marks its own work reviewed. Only a named person can do that.
It never takes a side. Where Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readings differ, Logia shows the readings and lets them speak.

rules.title: Editorial rules
rules.heading: How texts get into Logia
rules.dek: The rules every text in Logia follows, and the rights each work is used under, so anyone can check them.
rules.description: Logia's editorial rules: copied word for word from public-domain editions, scan fixes in the open, nothing marked reviewed by AI, and the rights basis of every work.
rules: Every excerpt is copied from a public-domain edition exactly as it reads, and the source it came from is saved beside it. Nothing is paraphrased, summarised, modernised or filled in from memory. A script checks every excerpt against its source on every change.

Text and translation must be published in 1930 or earlier, which makes them public domain in the United States. Each work records its edition, translator and year, and what is still to confirm for use worldwide. Logia copies from scans and open transcriptions, not from sites that claim rights in their typed editions.
Greek and Hebrew are never retyped
Original-language words appear only as the source prints them. Where a scan turns Greek into noise, the Greek is left out and the cut is marked, rather than typed in by hand.
Scan misreadings are corrected in the open

An excerpt keeps the scan's text. A misreading is fixed by a listed correction (“Let ns” → “Let us”), applied when the site is built. Only what the printed page plainly says is fixed; anything uncertain is left alone.
Places, citations and links are read from the sources
Where an excerpt sits in its work, the Scripture it cites and the Fathers a catena quotes are found by scripts from the sources, not typed. Each stays marked as unchecked until a person checks it.
Nothing is marked reviewed by an AI
Works, biographies, guides and translations stay drafts until a named person reviews them, and the site marks them so.
The Bible text is imported, never edited
Logia reads the Open Word Bible at a pinned version. A problem with its wording is raised with the Open Word Bible, not changed here.
Every tradition, in its own words

Logia sets Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant voices side by side and takes no side where they differ. A commentator's words are kept whole, even when harsh or dated; a note may explain, but nothing is cut silently.

items.new-covenant: The new covenant in my blood

justification.heading: Justification and faith
justification.dek: Abraham's faith counted as righteousness in Genesis, and Paul's words in Romans on the righteousness of God, being justified by faith, and peace with God.

items.gospel: The righteous shall live by faith
items.apart: The righteousness of God apart from the law
items.reckoned: Abraham believed, and it was counted to him as righteousness

grace-and-law.heading: The law and grace
grace-and-law.dek: Jesus on fulfilling the law, John on the law given through Moses, and Paul on what the law does.

items.fulfil: Not to abolish but to fulfil
items.moses: The law through Moses, grace and truth through Jesus Christ
items.knowledge: Through the law comes knowledge of sin
items.end: Christ the end of the law

election.heading: Election and predestination
election.dek: The passages on God's choosing: those the Father gives to the Son, those he foreknew, Jacob and Esau, and the remnant chosen by grace.

items.given: All that the Father gives me

the-cross.heading: The cross
the-cross.dek: Psalm 22, the crucifixion in Matthew, Luke and John, and Paul on Christ's death for sinners.

items.forsaken: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
items.paradise: Today you will be with me in paradise

resurrection.heading: The resurrection of Jesus
resurrection.dek: The empty tomb in Matthew and John, the road to Emmaus, Thomas, and Paul on Christ raised for our justification.

items.tomb: He is not here, he is risen
items.dies-no-more: Christ being raised dies no more

holy-spirit.heading: The Holy Spirit
holy-spirit.dek: Jesus's promise of the Spirit in John's farewell discourse, the Spirit breathed on the disciples, and Paul on the Spirit who dwells in believers.

items.teach: He will teach you all things
items.convict: When the Spirit of truth comes
items.indwelling: The Spirit of God dwells in you

prayer.heading: Prayer
prayer.dek: The Lord's Prayer in Matthew and Luke, asking and seeking, the persistent widow, praying in Jesus's name, Jesus's own prayer in John 17, and the Spirit who helps us pray.

items.in-my-name: Whatever you ask in my name
items.groanings: We do not know what to pray for

love.heading: The commandment to love
love.dek: Love of enemies, the greatest commandment, the good Samaritan, Jesus's new commandment, and love as the fulfilling of the law.

items.fulfilling: Love is the fulfilling of the law

peter.heading: Peter
peter.dek: Simon named Cephas, the call by the lake, the rock and the keys of the kingdom, Jesus's prayer for Peter, and Peter restored after the resurrection.
peter.note: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers understand the rock and the keys differently; every commentator in Logia on each passage is here.

items.fishers: From now on you will catch people

repentance.heading: Repentance and forgiveness
repentance.dek: David's prayer for mercy in Psalm 51, the blessing of forgiven sin in Psalm 32, the prodigal son, the Pharisee and the tax collector, and forgiving seventy times seven.

items.miserere: Have mercy on me, O God
items.blessed: Blessed is the one whose sin is forgiven
items.tax-collector: The Pharisee and the tax collector

shepherd.heading: The Good Shepherd
shepherd.dek: The Lord is my shepherd in Psalm 23, the lost sheep in Luke, the good shepherd who lays down his life in John, and Peter told to feed the sheep.
